After cutting cucumber if salt is added, then water comes out due to : (a) Active transport (b) Passive transport (c) Osmosis (d) Diﬀ usion U.P. P.C.S. (Pre) 2021 Ans. (c) Osmosis is the process when water (or solvent) molecules move from a region (solution) of low concentration to a region(solution) of higher concentration through a semi- permeable membrane. When salt is applied to cucumber or cut onion pieces, it makes their surrounding more concentrated than the concentration of their cell sap. Then it causes the water molecules in the cells of the cucumber and the cut onion pieces to move to the surrounding through their cell membrane (which is semipermeable). 17. Consider the following statements : 1. During the process of osmosis, the solvent travels from the concentrated solution to the dilute solution. 2. In the reverse osmosis, external pressure is applied to the dilute solution. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 I.A.S. (Pre) 2005 Ans. (d) In the process of osmosis, the solvent moves through a semi-permeable membrane into a region of higher solute concentration from lower concentration to equalize the solute concentration on two sides. While in reverse osmosis, we apply external pressure upon concentrated solution to reverse the movement of solvent, i.e. from more concentrated to weaker dilute solution. Match List-I (oxidation number) with List-II (the element) and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists : List-I List-II A. 2 1. Oxidation number of Mn in MnO2 B. 3 2. Oxidation number of S in H2SO4 C. 4 3. Oxidation number of Ca in CaO D. 6 4. Oxidation number of Al in NaAlH4 Code : A B C D (a) 3 4 1 2 (b) 4 3 1 2 (c) 3 4 2 1 (d) 4 3 2 1 I.A.S. (Pre) 2002 Ans. (a) The oxidation number of any compound is always zero. This means that sum of the oxidation number of all the elements present in the compound is zero. By this rule, we can now ﬁ nd the oxidation number in given options here – (1) Suppose, the oxidation number of Mn in MnO2 is x. MnO2 contains two oxygen ions, each with an oxidation number (–2). ⇒ x + 2 × (–2) = 0 x – 4 = 0 ⇒ x = 4 (2) Suppose, the oxidation number of S in H2SO4 is x. H2SO4 contains two hydrogen ion, each with an oxidation number (+1) and oxidation number of oxygen (–2). 2 (+1) + x + 4 (–2) = 0 ⇒ 2 + x – 8 = 0 ⇒ x = 6 (3) The oxidation number of Ca in CaO when oxygen has oxidation number (–2) ⇒ x – 2 = 0 ⇒ x = 2 (4) Suppose, the oxidation number of Al in NaAlH4 is x. NaAlH4 contains one Na which has oxidation number (+1) and four H which has oxidation number (–1). ⇒ (+1) + x + 4 (–1) = 0 ⇒ 1 + x – 4 = 0 ⇒ x = 3 25. Chromatography may be preparative or analytical. The purpose of preparative chromatography is to separate the components of a mixture for more advanced use and thus it is a form of puriﬁ cation. 20. Join − https://t.me/thehindu000 G–262 General Studies General Science Inorganic Chemistry Notes Classiﬁ cation of Elements x Periodic Table or Periodic table of elements is a tabular arrangement of the chemical elements, arranged by atomic number, electron conﬁ guration and recurring chemical properties, whose structure shows periodic trends. Need for classiﬁ cation of Elements : x Before the beginning of the 18th century, only a few elements were known, so it was quite easy to study and remember the properties of those elements and their compounds individually. x Later on, with the increasing number of elements, it became more and more diﬃ cult to study their properties individually, therefore the need for their classiﬁ cation was felt. Development of Periodic Table : x Several major attempts made for classiﬁ cation of elements. Some of them are as follows - (i) Prout Hypothesis (1815) - x William Prout observed that the atomic weights that had been measured for the elements known at that time appeared to be whole multiples of the atomic weight of hydrogen. x He hypothesized that the hydrogen atom was the only truly fundamental object, which he called protyle and that the atoms of other elements were actually groupings of various numbers of hydrogen atoms. x This postulation was discarded when the atomic weight of elements not found in the whole number. (ii) Dobereiner’s Triads (1829) - x According to this law, when chemically analogous elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic mass, they formed well-marked group of three called ‘Triads’, in which the atomic mass of middle element was nearly equal to the arithmetic mean of the other. x Examples of triads of elements are as follows - Element Atomic Mass Mean of 1 & 3 1. 2. 3. Lithium Sodium Potassium 7 23 39 = 23 1. 2. 3. Calcium Strontium Barium 40 88 137 = 88.5 x This classiﬁ cation did not receive wide acceptance since only a few elements could be arranged into triads. (iii) Newlands’ Law of Octaves (1865) - x If the chemical elements are arranged according to increasing atomic weight, those with similar physical and chemical properties occur after each interval of seven elements. x Arrangement of some elements with their atomic weights according to the Law of Octaves - Li Be B C N O F (7) (9) (11) (12) (14) (16) (19) Na Mg Al Si P S Cl (23) (24) (27) (28) (31) (32) (35.5) x Newlands contributed the word ‘periodic’ in chemistry. (iv) Lothar Meyer’s Atomic Volume Curve (1869) - x Lothar Meyer, a German chemist plotted a graph between atomic weight and atomic volume (i.e. atomic weight in solid state / density), he found that elements with similar properties occupied the similar position on the graph. (v) Mendeleev’s Periodic Table - x “The physical and chemical properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic mass”. Salient Features of Mendeleev’s Periodic Table (i) Mendeleev arranged the elements in the increasing order of their atomic mass. (ii) The elements are arranged in horizontal rows called periods. Those are six in numbers (1 to 6 - Arabic numerals). Period 4th, 5th & 6th have two series of elements. (iii) The vertical columns are called groups. There are eight groups numbered from I to VIII (Roman Numerals). (iv) Groups I to VII are further divided into A & B subgroups. However, group VIII contains three elements in each of the three periods. (v) All the elements present in a particular group are chemically similar in nature. They also show a regular gradation in their physical and chemical properties form top to bottom. (vi) Mendeleev’s classiﬁ cation included all the 63 elements known at that time. (vii) He left blank spaces for elements yet to be discovered, which were filled with the discovery of germanium, scandium and gallium. Join − https://t.me/thehindu000 General Science General Studies G–263 (vi) Modern Periodic Table - x Keeping in view the drawbacks of Mendeleev’s periodic table such as anomalous pair - placing of heavier element before lighter one and there is no place for diﬀ erent isotopes of an element in the periodic table, it was felt that the arrangement of elements in the periodic table should be based on some other property which is more fundamental than atomic mass. x Moseley (1913) arranged the elements in a tabular form based on their atomic numbers. x It states that the chemical and physical properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number i.e if elements are arranged in the order of their increasing atomic number, the elements with similar properties are repeated after certain regular intervals. (vii) Long Form of Periodic Table - x The accepted modern periodic table is the Long form of Periodic Table. x The arrangement of elements in this table is also in keeping with their electronic structure (conﬁ guration). Columns represent the Groups or family and rows represent the Periods. Groups x It contains 18 vertical columns. The groups have been numbered from 1 to 18 (in Arabic numerals). x All elements present in a group generally have similar electronic conﬁ guration in their valence shell and have a same number of valence electrons. Periods x There are seven horizontal rows in the modern periodic table. x The elements in a period have consecutive atomic numbers. x The periods have been numbered form 1 to 7 (Arabic numerals). x In each period a new shell starts ﬁ lling up. The period number is also the number of shells which starts ﬁ lling up as we move from left to right across the period. (a) The ﬁ rst period is the shortest period of all. It contains only two elements - H and He. (b) The second and third periods are called short-periods each with 8 elements. (c) The 4th & 5th periods are called long periods each with 18 elements. (d) The 6th & 7th periods are called very long periods containing 32 elements each. Types of Elements 1. Main Group Elements or Normal Elements - x Main Group elements have been placed in groups 1 and 2 on the left side and in groups 13 to 17 on the right side of the periodic table. x Their outermost shell is incomplete (their outermost shell has less than eight electrons). 2. Noble Gases - x Group 18 contains noble gases. Their outermost shell contains 8 electrons except Helium (only 2 electron in the outermost shell). x These are inert gases (do not react) and with zero valency. 3. Transition Elements (d-block elements) - x Groups 3 to 12 contain transition elements. x Their two outermost shells are incomplete. x All these elements are metals with high melting and boiling points, they are a good conductor of heat and electricity, magnetic and exhibit variable valancies. 4. Inner Transition Elements (f-block elements)- x These have been shown separately below the main periodic table. x Their three outermost shells are incomplete. x There are two series of 15 elements. a . Lanthanoids (4f) x This series consists of 15 elements from Atomic No. 57 to 71 (La to Lu). x These are all placed in group 3, period 6. x These elements, along with the chemically similar elements scandium and yttrium, are often collectively known as the 'rare earth elements'. b . Actinoids (5f) x It consists of elements from atomic number 89 to 103 (Ac to Lr). x These are all placed in group 3, Period 7. x All actinoids are radioactive and release energy upon radioactive decay. x The element Lanthanum (57) and Actinium (89) are the eponyms of Lanthanoid and Actinoid series respectively. x Even though lanthanoid means like lanthanum and actinoid means like actinium and as such they should not be included in these groups but IUPAC acknowledges their inclusion based on common usage. x Sometimes these groups are considered to have 14 elements each (without lanthanum and actinium).
